content: Souroti is a rural village located in the Thessaloniki prefecture of Greece, approximately 25 kilometers (16 miles) from the city of Thessaloniki. The village is particularly renowned for its mineral water, which is bottled locally. Administratively, Souroti is part of the municipality of Vasilika. Historically, Souroti was established as an immigrant village following the Balkan Wars and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. Before 1912, the area was known as Surukli, a name derived from the Turkish word suru, meaning herd. At that time, the land was owned by five Turkish landlords who sold it to Jewish buyers from Thessaloniki. The first Greek settlers in the area were the Christos Lolas family, originally shepherds from Vlasti in the Kozani prefecture. They sold their sheep to purchase the land from the Jewish owners. In 1914, forty families of Arvanites, who were bilingual in Greek and Arvanitika, arrived from Mandritsa in North Thrace after a Bulgarian invasion of their village. These families primarily engaged in silk production, utilizing the local mulberry trees. In 1922, following the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, approximately 48 families from Asia Minor settled in Souroti. These families originated from regions such as Izmir, Aydin, Bursa, Kyos, Mudanya, and Eastern Thrace. They were well-educated and brought their own cultural traditions. In Souroti, they worked in silk production, olive oil production, and viticulture. Between 1928 and 1930, additional Vlach shepherds from Vlasti and a few Sarakatsanoi families also settled in the area. The Greek state distributed land to these immigrants in 1914 and again in 1932. The community of Souroti was officially recognized by the Greek state on September 20, 1947. Since then, the village has experienced steady development, with agriculture and the bottling of mineral water serving as its primary economic activities. In 1997, as part of the Kapodistrias Plan, a major reorganization of local self-government, Souroti merged with the municipality of Vasilika, along with other nearby communities such as Agia Paraskevi, Agios Antonios, Livadi, Monopigado, and Peristera. In recent years, people from Thessaloniki have begun moving to the area, and Souroti is expected to evolve into a suburb of the city. The discovery of the mineral water spring in Souroti dates back to the time when the area was still part of the Ottoman Empire. The land around the current bottling facility was originally a swamp, and the spring was unknown. During World War I in 1915, French troops camping in the area, then called Surukli, mapped the spring and constructed a basic bottling facility. In 1917, Serbian troops also camped in the area and built a new bottling facility, referring to the water as Sour Water (Kisela Voda). In 1918, the Lolas family took over and refurbished the facility. By 1925, George Chonaios acquired the enterprise and operated it as a private business, allocating 5% of the profits to the local community. The company went public in 1998, leading to rapid growth and making Souroti one of the most popular mineral water brands in Greece. Souroti mineral water is classified as a sub-acidic sparkling mineral water rich in calcium and magnesium, as per Greek legislation (Government Gazette 600/1-8-1991, Decision No 4). It is also listed as a Natural Mineral Water by the European Union. Historically, the water was naturally sparkling, but carbon dioxide is now added during bottling to maintain its effervescence. The water originates from a source approximately 150 meters underground and owes its high quality to the geological formations of Mount Anthemounta, which consist of semi-metamorphic, metamorphic, and igneous rocks. As the water flows slowly through these rock formations, it is naturally filtered and enriched with beneficial minerals, resulting in its unique composition and taste. The water from the spring is naturally cold, maintaining a steady temperature of around 16°C. It is characterized by a high magnesium content, an ideal calcium-to-magnesium ratio, and low levels of sodium and nitrates. Additionally, it contains potassium, fluorine, and trace elements such as iron, copper, manganese, lithium, selenium, chromium, and zinc. Souroti water is known for its exceptional taste and is highly palatable. It supports the proper functioning of the digestive and urinary systems and offers various health benefits. One liter of Souroti water provides approximately one-quarter of the daily recommended intake of calcium and magnesium. This distinguishes it from soda water, which is simply potable water with added sodium bicarbonate to mimic the properties of natural mineral water.
